summary: This RFC describes a pseudowire mechanism for carrying a packet service over an MPLS network when the client label switching router and the provider edge equipment are in the same box. It can carry the layer 2 and layer 3 protocols needed between the clients.

eli5.summary: It is a tunnel inside one device, where two parts act like they are linked by a long cable.

questions: what is packet pseudowire over mpls
how to carry packet services over an mpls psn
how does a packet pw carry ip over mpls
subtitle: How to carry IP, MPLS and their support protocols between two routers over a pseudowire by using a virtual Ethernet link.

tldr.problem: Two client MPLS routers need to talk across a provider's MPLS network as if directly linked, exchanging IP, link-layer and MPLS traffic, while staying isolated from the provider's network.
tldr.mechanism: The client router sits inside the provider edge equipment and wraps each packet in an Ethernet header. The packet then travels over an Ethernet Raw Mode pseudowire (PW type 5), set up as described for Ethernet PWs in RFC 4448.
tldr.outcome: The pseudowire looks like a single point-to-point link to the client layer. The RFC chose this design over three alternatives because it needs no new forwarding design and already runs on much existing hardware.

today: RFC 6658 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata.

sections.title: Why a Packet Pseudowire
sections.content:
RFC 6658 describes a way to carry a packet service over an MPLS packet switched network (PSN) while keeping the client network and the server network isolated from each other. The server network may be an MPLS network or one conforming to the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). The client may be either as well.

Two adjacent MPLS label switching routers (LSRs) do not simply swap MPLS packets. They also exchange IP packets for adjacency formation, control, routing, label exchange, management and monitoring. They may exchange data-link packets too, such as IS-IS Hellos and Link-Layer Discovery Protocol frames. So the attachment between them has to multiplex several protocols, and all of those protocols must fate share.

The RFC covers the case where the client LSR and the server Provider Edge (PE) are co-located in the same equipment. There the data-link layer can be simplified to a point-to-point Ethernet that multiplexes the various data-link types onto a pseudowire.
sections.eli5: Two routers need to chat in many languages at once over a path they do not own. The trick is to give them one shared envelope style that can hold all of those messages.

sections.title: The Network Reference Model
sections.content:
The model extends the PWE3 architecture of RFC 3985. The client LSRs (LSR1 and LSR2) belong to the client MPLS PSN. The PEs (PE1 and PE2) belong to the server PSN that provides the connectivity between them.

The attachment circuit joining each LSR to its PE is a virtual interface within the equipment. A packet pseudowire provides connectivity between these virtual interfaces and transports all the required layer 2 and layer 3 protocols between LSR1 and LSR2.

To the client layer, the packet PW appears as a single point-to-point link. Adjacency formation and maintenance follow normal client-layer practice. Metrics for the link are a client-layer matter. If the client uses the PW as part of a traffic-engineered path, the client operator must make sure the server-layer operator provides the necessary service-level agreement.
sections.eli5: Inside each box, the router and the tunnel end are connected by an imaginary plug. The two routers then believe they are joined by one plain cable.

sections.title: The Forwarding Model
sections.content:
Forwarding works like a VPN: a decision is made at the client layer, an encapsulation is applied, and then a second decision is made at the server layer. A packet PW PE has three components: the client LSR, a PW processor and a server LSR.

For comparison, an ordinary Ethernet PW (RFC 4448) has no client LSR. Packets arrive on the attachment circuit, the PW function optionally pushes the control word and then pushes the PW label. The server LSR function pushes the label needed to reach the egress PE.

For the packet PW, the embedded client LSR finds its next hop and pushes the client label. It then puts the packet in an Ethernet header with the Ethertype set to MPLS and hands it to the right PW instance. From there the PW instance proceeds as for an Ethernet PW.

At the egress PE, the server LSR uses the PW label to pick the PW instance, which processes the packet as RFC 4448 describes. The resulting Ethernet-encapsulated client packet goes to the egress client LSR. The RFC notes that the model is similar for an IP packet or any other protocol type.
sections.eli5: First the sender's router puts a letter in a standard envelope. Then the tunnel adds its own outer wrapping. At the far end the wrappings come off in reverse order.

sections.title: Packet PW Encapsulation
sections.content:
The client network-layer packet (n octets) is preceded by a 14-octet Ethernet header, an optional 4-octet control word, a 4-octet PW label and one or more server MPLS tunnel labels at 4 octets each. This conforms to the PW protocol stack of RFC 4448.

The stack does not keep 32-bit alignment between the virtual Ethernet header and the control word (or the PW label when the control word is absent). The RFC says this loss is necessary to stay backwards compatible with the Ethernet PW design.

Ethernet Raw Mode (PW type 5) MUST be used for the packet PW. PEs MAY use a local Ethernet address, or the two special addresses PacketPWEthA and PacketPWEthB that IANA allocated. When RFC 4447 signaling sets up the PW, the two LDP peers compare their IP addresses numerically: the PE with the higher address uses PacketPWEthA and the other uses PacketPWEthB. With no signaling protocol, suitable Ethernet addresses MUST be configured at each PE.

Peers MUST be prepared to handle a multicast destination address in the Ethernet header, because some client-layer protocols require it even though the PW is point to point.
sections.eli5: The message goes in an envelope with an address label, then a tunnel ticket, then outer route stickers. Each wrapper is a small fixed size.

sections.title: Ethernet Restrictions and Congestion
sections.content:
Ethernet is used here as a convenience, since the hardware is widely available. Only its protocol multiplexing is needed. A server LSR is therefore not required to implement Ethernet OAM.

VLANs, IEEE 802.1p and IEEE 802.1Q tagging between PEs are not supported. Point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-multipoint operation of the virtual Ethernet are not supported either.

On congestion, a packet PW normally carries IP, MPLS and their support protocols, so nothing beyond the usual IP or MPLS considerations applies. If it carries other protocols at higher volumes, the congestion considerations developed for PWs (RFC 3985 and RFC 5659) apply.
sections.eli5: The tunnel only borrows the Ethernet envelope for sorting mail. It does not use the fancy extras like separate lanes.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says the virtual Ethernet approach to packet PW introduces no new security risks. It points to RFC 3985, RFC 4447 and RFC 3916 for a fuller discussion of pseudowire security.

IANA allocated two unicast Ethernet addresses from the IANA Unicast 48-bit MAC Addresses registry: 00-00-5E-00-52-00 for PacketPWEthA and 00-00-5E-00-52-01 for PacketPWEthB.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added that could be a danger. Two special mailbox names were reserved so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Alternatives Considered
sections.content:
Appendix A records four candidate designs that the PWE3 Working Group analyzed.

  • Protocol identifier in the control word: the most compact stack and simple, but a new forwarding design that may not deploy on many existing platforms, and it offers no advantage over virtual Ethernet beyond a smaller header.
  • PID label: a label after the PW label naming the protocol. It fits the MPLS architecture, but many designs assume a forwarding decision uses a single label, and many commodity chip sets could not support it.
  • Parallel PWs: one PW per protocol. It is simple to forward, but protocols no longer fate share, OAM is harder, and managing a group of PWs as one adds control-plane complexity.
  • Virtual Ethernet: conceptually simple, already implemented in many hardware platforms, at the cost of a larger MTU and a full Ethernet adjacency.

The authors concluded that virtual Ethernet, being a well-known stack on existing hardware, is the most attractive solution.
sections.eli5: The authors tried four ways to build the tunnel. They picked the one that reuses parts that already exist, so nobody needs to buy new equipment.
